title: GPT & Auto Essay Marking
author: Chris Wheadon
summary: Chris Wheadon revisits whether GPT can mark essays reliably, a year after he and Daisy Christodoulou concluded that its marks were erratic and its rationales little more than pastiche of the mark scheme. He examines a recent academic paper claiming high agreement between a fine-tuned GPT-3.5 model and human markers, noting that the appendices give enough detail to reproduce part of the method. The rubric in question awards language marks by counting spelling and grammar errors, which he argues reflects a non-educationalist view of writing and punishes ambition and flair. When he runs the paper's own prompts on GCSE essays, GPT miscounts errors, flags non-errors, and awards marks that contradict the rubric. He concludes that the headline kappa is unverifiable because it relies on a fine-tuned model that is not available, and that even the simplest rubric exceeds GPT's competence. The piece is a model of reading assessment research critically, testing claims against the appendix rather than the abstract.
points: Models seem to produce only weak correlations with human marks and cannot discriminate between more than three or four levels, whatever the headline claims.
Reading the appendices and trying to reproduce a paper's method is what exposes weak claims, since the detail is where they fail.
Marking writing by counting discrete spelling and grammar errors punishes ambition and atomises teaching, which is why comparative judgement was adopted for primary writing.
GPT cannot reliably count, so rubrics built on error counts produce marks that contradict the mark scheme itself.
A high kappa from a model fine-tuned on 80 percent of the data and tested on the remaining 20 percent cannot be verified without access to that model.
quotes: I have learned, however, that the detail of these papers is critical. In this case the Appendices give an admirable level of detail that allow us to attempt to reproduce some of their methodology.
As soon as you reduce writing to discrete elements of spelling and grammar you punish ambition, flair and creativity and begin to atomise your teaching.

However, leaving all that aside(!), I was intrigued as to whether GPT, which is notoriously bad at maths, could actually mark to this rubric. Using the same prompts and model as the authors I quickly found out that GPT still can’t count.
My count of how many times the GPT model believes there is an error is 18. So, you might say, anyone could fail to count them up correctly, which is a fair point.

If GPT were an examiner, they would immediately be stopped while the Chief got on the phone to ask what on earth they were thinking. The feedback on this essay was quite typical for all the essays I gave it.

Apparently the high kappa reported by the authors was achieved by fine-tuning the GPT model on 80% of the data-set of essays the authors used, and then marking the final 20% using the fine-tuned model. As the trained model hasn’t been made available to us it would be impossible to verify this claim, but what is clear is that even with the simplest possible rubric GPT fails to get close to a basic level of competence.
